subject_line: A blue glaucus drifting through Blue: Dragon of the Sea
email_body:
Dear Aleesah,

I came across Blue: Dragon of the Sea, your new Wombat Books picture book with Tamlyn Teow, and was struck by your choice of hero: the blue glaucus, a tiny nudibranch also called the Sea Swallow, rather than a more familiar ocean animal. After more than sixty-five books, I'd love to ask how you decide which overlooked creature deserves its own story, and how you balance fact with narrative.

subject_line: Art-making as subject in Test Piece
email_body:
Dear Sheryda,

I've been reading about Test Piece, your Coach House collection that was a finalist for the 2023 Dorothy Livesay Poetry Prize, and its poems that turn to the process and practice of art-making through abstract minimalist artists. Coming after Hard Feelings and Floating Is Everything, it seems to shift attention from feeling itself toward how a thing gets made. I'd love to ask what drew you to those artists, and whether watching them work changed your own drafting or teaching at UBC.

subject_line: Del Hanks and the manuscript inside Black Star
email_body:
Dear Maureen,

I've been reading about Black Star, your Anvil Press novel that won the CAA Fred Kerner Book Award, and its narrator Del Hanks: forty, on the verge of tenure, and writing what is framed as her own manuscript on the moral philosophy of difficult choices. As with The Tracey Fragments, one unstable voice carries the book. I'd love to ask how you built a novel that pretends to be an academic text, and how your third novel is taking shape.

book_title: The Double Life of Benson Yu
subject_line: The narrator who keeps interrupting Benson Yu
email_body:
Dear Kevin,

I've been reading about The Double Life of Benson Yu, and especially the choice to let the comic-book creator narrating it keep breaking in from the present, struggling over whether to continue the story of young Benny and Constantine. Reviewers split on that metafictional layer, and the Ottawa Review of Books called the rewards for perseverance grand. I'd love to ask why the book needed an author arguing with his own material, and how you found the right distance between the two Bensons.

subject_line: From My Body Is Yours to the poems of Bad Ideas
email_body:
Dear Michael,

I've been looking at the range of your books, from the novels Cumberland and Progress to My Body Is Yours, your Arsenal Pulp Press memoir about breaking out of gender norms and free of a hurtful past, which was a Lambda Literary Award finalist, and now the poems of Bad Ideas. I'd love to ask how moving between memoir and poetry changes what you're willing to say about the body, and how teaching creative writing at UBC Okanagan feeds back into your own work.

subject_line: Sophie, Alex and Maggie in Mudflowers
email_body:
Dear Aley,

I've been reading about Mudflowers, your Rare Machines debut that was a finalist for the 2023 BMO Winterset Award, and its Toronto artist Sophie, grieving her mother while moving between her childhood friend Alex and the poet Maggie until secrets begin to give way beneath both relationships. I'd love to ask how grief and divided love shaped the book's structure, and how writing from Corner Brook, with The Horse and a second novel underway, compares with writing that first Toronto story.

subject_line: From Oppenheimer's Los Alamos to Soldiers, Hunters, Not Cowboys
email_body:
Dear Aaron,

I've been following the arc of your Coach House novels, from Y: Oppenheimer, Horseman of Los Alamos, which Rachel Martinez carried into French for La Peuplade, to Soldiers, Hunters, Not Cowboys in 2023. Oppenheimer as a subject also sits interestingly beside your current research on frontier AI at Memorial. I'd love to ask how scholarship and fiction trade ideas in your practice, and what it was like to see Oppenheimer's voice reworked in another language.

subject_line: De Calmi à quatre-vingt-dix romans jeunesse
email_body:
Bonjour Martine,

En lisant votre parcours, j'ai été frappé par le chemin parcouru depuis Calmi, votre premier roman pour adultes en 1996, puis Simon, l'espion amoureux en 1999 : on parle aujourd'hui de près de quatre-vingt-dix romans pour jeunes lecteurs. Dans Québec français, vous décriviez une écriture par blocs d'environ trois mois, suivis des commentaires de l'éditeur. J'aimerais vous demander si cette méthode a changé avec les années, et ce que les rencontres dans les écoles apportent à vos livres.

The Author Ledger est un projet indépendant qui publie de courts portraits d'auteurs. Chaque portrait se construit à partir de quelques questions écrites, auxquelles vous répondez à votre rythme, et le texte complet vous est soumis pour relecture avant publication.

subject_line: Du pirate Safran aux Échos d'école
email_body:
Bonjour Nadine,

En parcourant votre bibliographie, j'ai été frappé par son amplitude : de Plus tard, c'est quand ? chez Boomerang en 2006 et du pirate Safran jusqu'à Qui a pris mon crayon ?, troisième tome de la série Échos d'école aux Éditions Z'ailées, en passant par En morceaux, votre recueil de poésie chez Soulières. J'aimerais vous demander comment votre formation en journalisme influence votre écriture pour les six-huit ans, et ce que le passage à la poésie vous a permis de dire autrement.

subject_line: Passer d'Ella à L'asile du Nord
email_body:
Bonjour Carine,

En parcourant vos livres, j'ai remarqué l'écart de ton entre la longue série Ella chez Boomerang, illustrée par Sabrina Gendron, et Camille, L'asile du Nord, votre roman d'horreur paru en 2023 chez le même éditeur, sans compter La triple vie de Charlie chez Michel Quintin et Bloc boy chez Andara. J'aimerais vous demander comment on dose la peur pour de jeunes lecteurs, et ce que vos heures du conte animées dans les écoles vous apprennent sur ce qui les accroche vraiment.

subject_line: Facing fear head on in Dragons Drumming
email_body:
Dear Sandra,

I came across Dragons Drumming, your rhyming picture book with Maya Bora from Rosella Ridge Books, and liked that a deliberately noisy story for toddlers is built around a real question: when you feel fear, do you run and hide, or face it head on? I'd love to ask how you shaped rhyme and rhythm to carry that idea for very young listeners, and how it differs from writing the Adamson Adventures chapter books, especially with your Canberra Writers Festival session this month.

subject_line: A rascally swamp wallaby in Where's Lucky?
email_body:
Dear Jacqui,

I came across Where's Lucky?, your Little Pink Dog Books story with Sandra Severgnini, and was drawn to the fact that its rascally swamp wallaby is based on real joey rescues; it went on to be shortlisted for the Speech Pathology Australia Book of the Year. Alongside it sit It's Time All Possums Went to Bed, read on Play School, and your nonfiction Australia Remembers: Wartime Nurses. I'd love to ask how you move between playful rhyme and wartime history.

subject_line: Three names, one writer: from End of the Night Girl to Best, First and Last
email_body:
Dear Amy,

I was interested to learn that you write literary fiction as Amy T. Matthews, romance as Tess LeSue and historical romance as Amy Barry, and that your path runs from End of the Night Girl, with its Australian waitress haunted by the ghost of a murdered Polish Jew, through Someone Else's Bucket List to Best, First and Last. I'd love to ask how each name changes the way you work, and how leading creative writing at Flinders shapes what you tell students about genre.
